title: Time, Speed and Distance
subtitle: Quantitative Aptitude – Placement Preparation
description: Learn the important formulas, shortcuts and placement-level applications of time, speed and distance, including average speed, relative speed, trains, races, circular tracks, boats and streams.
learningObjectives: Understand the relationship between time, speed and distance.
Convert speed between kilometres per hour and metres per second.
Solve direct speed, distance and time questions.
Understand the inverse relationship between speed and time.
Use relative speed for objects moving in the same or opposite directions.
Solve meeting, overtaking and catching-up problems.
Solve problems involving late and early arrival.
Apply placement shortcuts to solve questions quickly.

sections.heading: 1. Basic Concepts
content: Speed tells us how much distance an object covers in a given amount of time.
Distance is the total length travelled by an object.
Time is the duration taken to cover a distance.
Before applying a formula, ensure that the units of speed, distance and time are compatible.
formulas: Speed = Distance / Time
Distance = Speed × Time
Time = Distance / Speed

examples.question: A car covers 240 km in 4 hours. Find its speed.
A bus travels at 55 km/h for 6 hours. Find the distance travelled.
A person travels 180 km at 45 km/h. Find the time taken.

sections.heading: 2. Unit Conversion
content: Speed is commonly expressed in kilometres per hour or metres per second.
Convert the speed before solving when the units of distance and time are different.
The fraction 5/18 converts kilometres per hour into metres per second.
The fraction 18/5 converts metres per second into kilometres per hour.
formulas: 1 km = 1000 metres
1 hour = 3600 seconds
km/h to m/s: Multiply by 5/18
m/s to km/h: Multiply by 18/5

examples.question: Convert 72 km/h into m/s.
Convert 25 m/s into km/h.
A train moves at 54 km/h. How many metres does it cover in 20 seconds?

sections.heading: 3. Relationship Between Speed and Time
content: For a fixed distance, speed and time are inversely proportional.
If speed increases, the time required decreases.
If speed decreases, the time required increases.
When the distance remains constant, the product of speed and time remains constant.
formulas: For the same distance: Speed₁ × Time₁ = Speed₂ × Time₂
Speed₁ / Speed₂ = Time₂ / Time₁

examples.question: A journey takes 6 hours at 50 km/h. How long will it take at 75 km/h?
A person completes a journey in 8 hours at 45 km/h. What speed is required to complete it in 6 hours?

sections.heading: 4. Effect of Percentage Change in Speed
content: For a fixed distance, a percentage increase in speed produces a percentage decrease in time.
The percentage increase in speed and percentage decrease in time are not numerically equal.
Similarly, a reduction in speed increases the time taken.
formulas: If speed increases by x%, decrease in time = [x / (100 + x)] × 100%
If speed decreases by x%, increase in time = [x / (100 − x)] × 100%

examples.question: If speed increases by 25%, by what percentage does the time decrease?
If speed decreases by 20%, by what percentage does the time increase?
A person increases speed by 50%. Find the percentage reduction in travelling time.

sections.heading: 5. Average Speed
content: Average speed is not always the arithmetic mean of the given speeds.
It must be calculated using the total distance and total time.
The arithmetic mean can be used when an object travels for equal amounts of time at different speeds.
For equal distances travelled at two speeds, use the special equal-distance formula.
formulas: Average speed = Total distance / Total time
For equal time at speeds x and y: Average speed = (x + y) / 2
For equal distances at speeds x and y: Average speed = 2xy / (x + y)

examples.question: A car travels for 2 hours at 40 km/h and 3 hours at 60 km/h. Find its average speed.
examples.solution: Total distance = 2 × 40 + 3 × 60 = 80 + 180 = 260 km. Total time = 5 hours. Average speed = 260/5 = 52 km/h.

examples.question: A person travels equal distances at 40 km/h and 60 km/h. Find the average speed.
A cyclist travels for equal amounts of time at 30 km/h and 50 km/h. Find the average speed.
examples.solution: For equal time, average speed = (30 + 50)/2 = 40 km/h.

sections.heading: 6. Average Speed for Three Equal Distances
content: When three equal distances are covered at three different speeds, calculate total distance and total time.
Assume each equal distance to be a convenient common value or use the direct formula.
formulas: For three equal distances at speeds x, y and z: Average speed = 3xyz / (xy + yz + zx)

examples.question: A person covers three equal distances at 30 km/h, 40 km/h and 60 km/h. Find the average speed.

sections.heading: 7. Relative Speed
content: Relative speed describes how quickly the distance between two moving objects changes.
When objects move in opposite directions, their speeds are added.
When objects move in the same direction, the slower speed is subtracted from the faster speed.
Relative speed is used in meeting, overtaking, train and race questions.
formulas: Opposite directions: Relative speed = Speed₁ + Speed₂
Same direction: Relative speed = Faster speed − Slower speed
Time to meet or overtake = Initial distance / Relative speed

examples.question: Two cars move in opposite directions at 50 km/h and 70 km/h. Find their relative speed.
Two cyclists move in the same direction at 24 km/h and 18 km/h. Find their relative speed.
Two vehicles are 300 km apart and move towards each other at 40 km/h and 60 km/h. When will they meet?

sections.heading: 8. Meeting Point Problems
content: When two people start at the same time from opposite ends and meet, they travel for equal durations.
Therefore, the ratio of the distances travelled is equal to the ratio of their speeds.
The meeting point divides the total distance according to the speed ratio.
formulas: Distance travelled by A / Distance travelled by B = Speed of A / Speed of B
Distance covered before meeting = Speed × Meeting time

examples.question: Two persons start from points 280 km apart and move towards each other at 30 km/h and 40 km/h. Find the meeting time.
examples.solution: Combined speed = 30 + 40 = 70 km/h. Meeting time = 280/70 = 4 hours.

examples.question: In the previous example, how far from the first point do they meet?
examples.solution: Distance travelled by the first person = 30 × 4 = 120 km.

examples.question: Two persons move towards each other at speeds in the ratio 3:5. Find the ratio of distances covered before meeting.
examples.solution: They travel for equal time. Therefore, the distance ratio is also 3:5.

sections.heading: 9. Catching and Overtaking
content: Overtaking occurs when a faster object moving in the same direction catches a slower object.
Use the difference of their speeds as the relative speed.
The faster object must cover the initial gap between them.
formulas: Overtaking time = Initial gap / (Faster speed − Slower speed)

examples.question: A car moving at 70 km/h is 60 km behind a bus moving at 50 km/h. How long will the car take to catch the bus?
A runner moving at 10 m/s is 100 metres behind another runner moving at 8 m/s. Find the catching time.

sections.heading: 10. Late and Early Arrival
content: These questions compare travelling times at two different speeds over the same distance.
At a lower speed, a person may arrive late.
At a higher speed, the person may arrive early.
The difference between the two travelling times equals the total difference between the late and early arrival times.
formulas: Distance = Time difference / [(1/Slow speed) − (1/Fast speed)]
If late by a minutes at one speed and early by b minutes at another speed, difference in travelling times = a + b minutes

examples.question: At 40 km/h, a person arrives 15 minutes late. At 50 km/h, the person arrives 15 minutes early. Find the distance.
examples.solution: Difference in time = 30 minutes = 1/2 hour. Distance × (1/40 − 1/50) = 1/2. Distance × 1/200 = 1/2. Distance = 100 km.

examples.question: A student walking at 4 km/h reaches college 10 minutes late, while at 5 km/h the student reaches 2 minutes early. Find the travelling-time difference.

sections.heading: 11. Stoppage Problems
content: A vehicle's speed while moving may be different from its overall average speed when stoppages are included.
Without stoppages, the vehicle covers more distance in one hour than it does when stoppages are included.
The difference can be used to calculate stopping time.
formulas: Distance lost per hour = Speed without stoppages − Speed with stoppages
Stoppage time per hour = [Distance lost / Speed without stoppages] × 60 minutes

examples.question: A bus travels at 60 km/h without stoppages and averages 48 km/h including stoppages. For how many minutes does it stop per hour?
examples.solution: Distance lost per hour = 60 − 48 = 12 km. Time to cover 12 km at 60 km/h = 12/60 hour = 12 minutes.

examples.question: A train runs at 80 km/h but its average speed including stoppages is 64 km/h. Find the stoppage time per hour.
examples.solution: Distance lost = 80 − 64 = 16 km. Stoppage time = 16/80 × 60 = 12 minutes.

sections.heading: 12. Race Problems
content: A race question compares the distances covered by competitors in the same time.
If A beats B by a certain distance, A completes the full race while B covers a smaller distance.
The ratio of their speeds equals the ratio of distances covered in the same time.
formulas: Speed of A / Speed of B = Distance covered by A / Distance covered by B
If A beats B by x metres in a d-metre race: Speed ratio A:B = d:(d − x)

examples.question: In a 200-metre race, A beats B by 20 metres. Find the ratio of their speeds.
examples.solution: When A covers 200 metres, B covers 180 metres. Speed ratio A:B = 200:180 = 10:9.

examples.question: In a 500-metre race, A beats B by 50 metres. If A's speed is 10 m/s, find B's speed.
examples.solution: Speed ratio A:B = 500:450 = 10:9. B's speed = 10 × 9/10 = 9 m/s.

examples.question: A runs 25% faster than B. In a 400-metre race, by how many metres does A beat B?
examples.solution: Speed ratio A:B = 125:100 = 5:4. When A covers 400 metres, B covers 400 × 4/5 = 320 metres. A beats B by 80 metres.

sections.heading: 13. Circular Track Problems
content: On a circular track, runners may move in the same direction or opposite directions.
They meet whenever the relative distance covered equals one complete track length.
For the first meeting, divide the track length by relative speed.
When lap times are given, the first return to the starting point together is found using the LCM of their lap times.
formulas: Same direction meeting time = Track length / Difference of speeds
Opposite direction meeting time = Track length / Sum of speeds
Time to meet at starting point again = LCM of individual lap times

examples.question: Two runners move around a 400-metre circular track in the same direction at 8 m/s and 6 m/s. When will the faster runner catch the slower runner?
Two runners move in opposite directions on a 500-metre track at 6 m/s and 4 m/s. Find their first meeting time.
Two runners complete one lap in 60 seconds and 90 seconds. When will they meet at the starting point again?
examples.solution: Required time = LCM of 60 and 90 = 180 seconds.

sections.heading: 14. Train Crossing a Pole or Person
content: When a train crosses a stationary pole, tree or person, it covers a distance equal to its own length.
Convert the train's speed into metres per second when length is given in metres and time in seconds.
formulas: Time to cross a pole = Length of train / Speed of train
Length of train = Speed × Time

examples.question: A 180-metre train moves at 54 km/h. How long does it take to cross a pole?
A train moving at 72 km/h crosses a pole in 15 seconds. Find its length.

sections.heading: 15. Train Crossing a Platform or Bridge
content: To completely cross a platform, the train must cover its own length plus the platform length.
The same rule applies to a bridge, tunnel or stationary object having a measurable length.
formulas: Distance covered = Train length + Platform length
Crossing time = (Train length + Platform length) / Train speed

examples.question: A 150-metre train moving at 54 km/h crosses a 300-metre platform. Find the time taken.
examples.solution: Total distance = 150 + 300 = 450 metres. Speed = 15 m/s. Time = 450/15 = 30 seconds.

examples.question: A 200-metre train crosses a 400-metre bridge in 24 seconds. Find its speed.
examples.solution: Total distance = 200 + 400 = 600 metres. Speed = 600/24 = 25 m/s = 25 × 18/5 = 90 km/h.

sections.heading: 16. Two Trains Crossing
content: When two trains completely cross each other, the required relative distance is the sum of their lengths.
For trains moving in opposite directions, add their speeds.
For trains moving in the same direction, subtract the slower speed from the faster speed.
formulas: Required distance = Length of first train + Length of second train
Opposite directions: Time = Sum of lengths / Sum of speeds
Same direction: Time = Sum of lengths / Difference of speeds

examples.question: Two trains of lengths 120 metres and 180 metres move in opposite directions at 54 km/h and 36 km/h. Find the crossing time.
examples.solution: Total length = 300 metres. Relative speed = 54 + 36 = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Time = 300/25 = 12 seconds.

examples.question: Two trains of lengths 150 metres and 250 metres move in the same direction at 72 km/h and 54 km/h. Find the overtaking time.
examples.solution: Total length = 400 metres. Relative speed = 72 − 54 = 18 km/h = 5 m/s. Time = 400/5 = 80 seconds.

sections.heading: 17. Train Crossing a Moving Person
content: When a train crosses a moving person, use relative speed.
The distance to be covered is the train's length because the person's physical length is ignored.
Add speeds if they move in opposite directions and subtract speeds if they move in the same direction.
formulas: Crossing time = Train length / Relative speed

examples.question: A 140-metre train moves at 54 km/h. A man walks in the same direction at 3.6 km/h. Find the time taken by the train to cross him.
examples.solution: Relative speed = 54 − 3.6 = 50.4 km/h = 14 m/s. Time = 140/14 = 10 seconds.

examples.question: A 180-metre train moves at 72 km/h while a person walks in the opposite direction at 18 km/h. Find the crossing time.
examples.solution: Relative speed = 72 + 18 = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Time = 180/25 = 7.2 seconds.

sections.heading: 18. Boats and Streams – Basic Concepts
content: The speed of a boat in still water is the speed of the boat when there is no current.
Downstream means travelling in the same direction as the stream.
Upstream means travelling against the direction of the stream.
The stream increases the boat's speed downstream and reduces its speed upstream.
formulas: Downstream speed = Speed of boat in still water + Speed of stream
Upstream speed = Speed of boat in still water − Speed of stream
Speed of boat in still water = (Downstream speed + Upstream speed) / 2
Speed of stream = (Downstream speed − Upstream speed) / 2

examples.question: The speed of a boat in still water is 12 km/h and the stream speed is 3 km/h. Find the downstream and upstream speeds.
examples.solution: Downstream speed = 12 + 3 = 15 km/h. Upstream speed = 12 − 3 = 9 km/h.

examples.question: A boat's downstream speed is 18 km/h and upstream speed is 10 km/h. Find the speed of the boat in still water.
A boat's downstream speed is 20 km/h and upstream speed is 12 km/h. Find the stream speed.

sections.heading: 19. Boats and Streams – Time and Distance
content: Use downstream speed for journeys made with the current.
Use upstream speed for journeys made against the current.
Calculate upstream and downstream times separately when a boat makes a return journey.
formulas: Downstream time = Distance / Downstream speed
Upstream time = Distance / Upstream speed
Total round-trip time = Downstream time + Upstream time

examples.question: A boat travels 45 km downstream at 15 km/h. Find the time taken.
A boat travels 36 km upstream at 9 km/h. Find the time taken.
A boat's speed in still water is 10 km/h and stream speed is 2 km/h. Find the total time to travel 24 km downstream and return.
examples.solution: Downstream speed = 12 km/h and upstream speed = 8 km/h. Downstream time = 24/12 = 2 hours. Upstream time = 24/8 = 3 hours. Total time = 5 hours.

sections.heading: 20. Rafts and Floating Objects
content: A raft, log or floating object has no independent speed of its own.
It moves only because of the stream.
Therefore, the speed of a floating object is equal to the speed of the stream.
formulas: Speed of raft = Speed of stream
Distance travelled by raft = Stream speed × Time

examples.question: A raft travels 18 km in 6 hours. Find the speed of the stream.
A log floats at 2.5 km/h. How far will it travel in 4 hours?

quickShortcuts.title: Basic formula triangle
quickShortcuts.note: Remember Distance = Speed × Time. Rearrange it to obtain speed or time.

quickShortcuts.title: Fixed distance
quickShortcuts.note: For the same distance, speed and time are inversely proportional.

quickShortcuts.title: Equal-distance average speed
quickShortcuts.note: For speeds x and y over equal distances, use 2xy/(x+y).

quickShortcuts.title: Equal-time average speed
quickShortcuts.note: For equal travelling times, use the arithmetic mean of the speeds.

quickShortcuts.title: Opposite directions
quickShortcuts.note: Add the speeds to obtain relative speed.

quickShortcuts.title: Same direction
quickShortcuts.note: Subtract the slower speed from the faster speed.

quickShortcuts.title: Train crossing a pole
quickShortcuts.note: The distance covered equals the length of the train.

quickShortcuts.title: Train crossing a platform
quickShortcuts.note: The distance covered equals train length plus platform length.

quickShortcuts.title: Two trains crossing
quickShortcuts.note: Add both train lengths and divide by their relative speed.

quickShortcuts.title: Boat speed
quickShortcuts.note: Boat speed in still water is half the sum of downstream and upstream speeds.

quickShortcuts.title: Stream speed
quickShortcuts.note: Stream speed is half the difference between downstream and upstream speeds.

quickShortcuts.title: Circular track
quickShortcuts.note: Use track length divided by relative speed for the first meeting.

quickShortcuts.title: Race speed ratio
quickShortcuts.note: Distances covered in the same time are in the same ratio as speeds.

commonMistakes: Using kilometres per hour directly with metres and seconds.
Forgetting to convert minutes into hours.
Taking the arithmetic mean for equal-distance average-speed questions.
Adding speeds when objects move in the same direction.
Subtracting speeds when objects move in opposite directions.
Using only the train length when crossing a platform.
Forgetting to add both train lengths when two trains cross.
Using train speed instead of relative speed when crossing a moving person.
Adding stream speed while travelling upstream.
Subtracting stream speed while travelling downstream.
Treating speed and time as directly proportional for a fixed distance.
Using the percentage increase in speed as the same percentage decrease in time.
Ignoring stoppage time while calculating overall average speed.
Using the entire track length incorrectly when solving circular-track meetings.

I can solve percentage-change questions involving speed and time.
I can calculate average speed using total distance and total time.
I know the equal-distance average-speed shortcut.
I can calculate relative speed in the same and opposite directions.
I can solve meeting and overtaking problems.
I can solve late-arrival and early-arrival questions.
I can solve race and circular-track problems.
I can calculate upstream and downstream speeds.
I can find the speed of a boat and the speed of a stream.
I can solve boat round-trip and raft questions.
